newsitem.title: UK: Ventspils seeks to beat off other Baltic hopefuls.
newsitem.headline: Ventspils seeks to beat off other Baltic hopefuls.

text.p: The Latvian oil port of Ventspils will see off threats to its role as the Baltic's primary exporter of Russian oil by moving ahead fast with its own expansion plans, senior Latvian officials said on Thursday.

"The Latvian transit corridor is the most rational route connecting oilfields in Russia with oil consumers in the West...We are concerned about the rush in planning and construction of new oil pipelines and terminals to the north and south of Latvia," Latvian President Guntis Ulmanis told a business seminar in London.
Expanding capacity at the ice-free port of Ventspils would be cheaper than any of the several other proposed oil export projects elsewhere in the region, the officials said.
These include the construction or expansion of oil terminals in Primorsk and Batareinaya Bay in Russia, at Muuga in Estonia and Porvoo in Finland.

All of these locations bear ice risk, particularly Primorsk, where ice forms early in the year and persists for six months, said William Arnold, chairman of oil project financing consultants William Arnold Associates.
"(Primorsk) is probably the dumbest place to put an oil port in the whole of the Baltic," said Arnold.
The tariff for transporting oil through Ventspils is $6.50 a tonne, half of that at the other proposed ports, he said.
Ventspils at its height handled 34 million tones of crude and products in 1987, but exports declined to a low of 16 million tonnes in 1992.

But exports are on the rise again. In 1995 the port handled 20 million tonnes of oil and the forecast for this year is 23 million tonnes, of which 14 million tonnes will be crude, said Janis Blazevics, President of Ventspils Nafta.
Dredging of the port to a depth of 17.5 metres, set for completion in the second half of 1997, will allow Ventspils to service tankers with a capacity of 120,000 tonnes, from 100,000 tonnes now.
Plans are also afoot for the expansion of pipeline capacity to the port.
In the short term, reconstruction of the existing crude pipeline supplying the port should boost capacity by some two million tonnes a year to 18 million tonnes.
This could be achieved with a "relatively small investment" and no need for external financing, said Blazevics.
But longer term, capacity could be increased by a further 12 to 18 million tonnes a year, said Latvian Transport Minister Vilis Kristopans.
"Our specialists have established four alternative versions of a pipeline development project to Ventspils," said Kristopans.

The cheapest proposal is a line running from Lithuania's Mazeikiai refinery which would involve the construction of 230 kilometres of pipeline and one pumping station, said Blazevics of Ventspils Nafta.
But even the most costly proposal would be a saving on the proposed site at Primorsk, officials said.
"Even the worst of Latvia's versions is saving almost $400 million of investment, or 18 percent, on the Primorsk project," said Transport Minister Kristopans.
A project implementation company comprising Latvian, Russian and Western interests is to be set up next year to put the proposals into action, Blazevics said.
-- Rosalind Russell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5387
